prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When Love with unconfinèd wings Hovers within my Gates, And my divine Althea brings To whisper at the Grates; When I lie tangled in her hair, And fettered to her eye, The Gods that wanton in the Air, Know no such Liberty. When flowing Cups run swiftly round With no allaying Thames, Our careless heads with Roses bound, Our hearts with Loyal Flames; When thirsty grief in Wine we steep, When Healths and draughts go free, Fishes that tipple in the Deep Know no such Liberty. When (like committed linnets) I With shriller throat shall sing The sweetness, Mercy, Majesty, And glories of my King; When I shall voice aloud how good He is, how Great should be, Enlargèd Winds, that curl the Flood, Know no such Liberty. Stone Walls do not a Prison make, Nor Iron bars a Cage; Minds innocent and quiet take That for an Hermitage. If I have freedom in my Love, And in my soul am free, Angels alone that soar above, Enjoy such Liberty.

Keywords: When, Love, Hovers

outputs.L1:
When Love, with unconfinèd wings,

outputs.L2:
Whenever Love, with wings that cannot be confined, drifts inside the boundaries of my prison, and my heavenly Althea comes near to speak softly through the bars, then—when I am caught in the strands of her hair and held fast by the power of her gaze—even the playful gods moving through the sky do not possess a freedom like mine.

When brimming cups are passed quickly from hand to hand, undiluted by the waters of the Thames; when our carefree brows are crowned with roses and our hearts burn with faithful devotion; when we drown our sorrow in wine and freely offer toasts and deep drinks, even the fish that drink within the ocean depths do not know such liberty.

When I, like a caged linnet, lift my voice more brightly in song, praising the sweetness, mercy, majesty, and splendor of my king; when I speak aloud of how good he is and how great he ought to be, then even the wide winds, released to ripple and bend the waters, have no freedom equal to mine.

Stone walls alone cannot truly create a prison, and iron bars do not by themselves make a cage. A calm and blameless mind can turn such a place into a quiet retreat. If I remain free in my love, and if my spirit is free within me, then only the angels who rise above the earth can share such liberty.
outputs.L3:
The speaker suggests that love gives him a powerful sense of freedom, even though he is physically confined in prison. His body may be trapped behind walls and bars, but his thoughts and emotions remain free because they are sustained by love. The presence of his beloved in his imagination allows him to rise above the limitations of his surroundings.

The speaker also finds comfort in wine, companionship, and loyal feeling. These pleasures help him move beyond grief and confinement, reminding him that imprisonment cannot completely take away joy or human connection. In moments of fellowship, he experiences a kind of emotional release that makes the prison seem less powerful.

His loyalty to the king also becomes a form of inner freedom. By singing the king’s praises, the speaker expresses his political and moral convictions. Even in prison, he can remain faithful to what he believes is right. This act of praise shows that his spirit has not been broken by confinement.

The speaker’s central argument is that “stone walls” and “iron bars” cannot truly imprison a mind that is innocent and peaceful. Physical barriers may restrict movement, but they cannot control a person’s conscience, imagination, or soul. Because he feels guiltless and remains inwardly calm, the speaker is not truly a prisoner in the deepest sense.

Ultimately, the speaker presents true freedom as something that comes from love and the soul rather than from physical circumstances. His inner liberty is so complete that he compares it to the freedom of angels. Through love, loyalty, and spiritual peace, he achieves a freedom that no prison can destroy.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the relationship between imprisonment and liberty by showing that true freedom does not depend only on the body’s physical condition. Although the speaker is confined in prison, he refuses to see himself as spiritually or emotionally defeated. Instead, he contrasts the narrowness of the prison with the richness of his inner life, remembering experiences of love, wine, loyalty, song, and devotion. These forms of inward freedom allow him to rise above the material limits of his cell.

Love is one of the poem’s strongest sources of liberty. When the speaker thinks of his beloved, Althea, visiting him or communicating with him, his prison seems to disappear. Her presence gives him a sense of emotional release, as though affection can open doors that no jailer can shut. Similarly, wine and fellowship represent another kind of freedom. In imagining himself drinking with loyal companions, the speaker feels connected to a wider community beyond the prison walls. Friendship and shared celebration become ways of resisting isolation.

The poem also connects freedom with political loyalty and song. The speaker’s devotion to his king and cause gives him a sense of purpose that cannot be taken away by imprisonment. Even if his body is controlled by others, his loyalty remains his own. Song, too, becomes a symbol of inner liberty, because it expresses joy, conviction, and spiritual independence. Through music and praise, the speaker’s mind and soul move beyond the physical space of the prison.

By the end of the poem, the speaker makes his central argument clear: external confinement cannot truly imprison someone whose conscience is innocent and whose spirit remains free. The famous lines about “stone walls” and “iron bars” declare that a prison is not defined simply by its walls or chains. If a person possesses inner peace, moral innocence, love, faith, and loyalty, then even a cell cannot become a true prison. The poem therefore presents liberty as an inward condition rather than merely an outward circumstance. In this sense, the speaker’s freedom is so complete that he compares it to the liberty of angels, suggesting a spiritual freedom beyond earthly power.
outputs.L5:
When love hovers, the world seems to pause between one heartbeat and the next.

It does not always arrive loudly. Sometimes it comes softly, like morning light slipping through a curtain, or the quiet comfort of someone staying when they could have left. It hovers in small gestures—a remembered favorite song, a hand reaching out in silence, a smile that says, “I understand.”

When love hovers, even ordinary moments feel touched by something sacred. A simple walk becomes a memory. A shared laugh becomes a shelter. The distance between two people feels smaller, as if the air itself is holding them together.

Love does not always need grand promises. Sometimes it is enough that it remains near, patient and warm, waiting to be noticed. And when love hovers over a life, it changes everything—not by force, but by presence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the full text of Richard Lovelace’s poem “To Althea, from Prison.”
counterfactuals.output:
**To Althea, from Prison**  
*by Richard Lovelace*

When Love with unconfined wings  
Hovers within my Gates;  
And my divine Althea brings  
To whisper at the Grates;  
When I lye tangled in her haire,  
And fetter’d to her eye,  
The Gods that wanton in the Aire,  
Know no such Liberty.

When flowing Cups run swiftly round  
With no allaying Thames,  
Our carelesse heads with Roses bound,  
Our hearts with Loyall Flames;  
When thirsty griefe in Wine we steepe,  
When Healths and draughts goe free,  
Fishes that tipple in the Deepe,  
Know no such Libertie.

When, like committed Linnets, I  
With shriller throat shall sing  
The sweetnes, Mercy, Majesty,  
And glories of my King;  
When I shall voyce aloud, how Good  
He is, how Great should be,  
Inlarged Winds, that curle the Flood,  
Know no such Liberty.

Stone Walls doe not a Prison make,  
Nor Iron bars a Cage;  
Mindes innocent and quiet take  
That for an Hermitage;  
If I have freedome in my Love,  
And in my soule am free;  
Angels alone that soar above,  
Enjoy such Liberty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
